A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same LEXAM benchmark. Their main text, tables, figures, mathematical material, and appendices A–J are readable and support reliable comparison, including content relocated or renumbered in v6.

before.justification: v4 reports original model evaluations, MCQ perturbation experiments, and judge validation using 50 question–answer pairs independently rated by three legal experts.

after.justification: v6 retains these original empirical results and adds evaluations of further models and judge ensembles.

M1.justification: The deployed evaluator remains the pointwise minimum of GPT-4o, DeepSeek-V3, and Qwen3-32B scores. Appendix E's answering and judging prompts are unchanged. Additional ensemble comparisons and explanations do not alter the proposed procedure.

E1.justification: Both versions use the same 2,841 open questions, 1,660 standard MCQs, and 385 perturbation questions from the same bilingual law-exam collection. Course renaming and newly documented selection details do not establish changed coverage; additional jurisdictions remain future plans.

E2.justification: Open-question comparisons expand from 26 to 36 models, adding Claude-4.5-Sonnet, Gemini-3-Pro-preview, three DeepSeek-V3.2 variants, GPT-OSS-20B/120B, Qwen3-Next, and Apertus-8B/70B. MCQ comparisons add five of these: Claude-4.5-Sonnet, DeepSeek-V3.2-Exp, both GPT-OSS models, and Qwen3-Next. Appendix G.4 also adds two judge-ensemble comparators.

E3.justification: Evaluation configurations expand to include GPT-OSS at 20B/120B, Apertus at 8B/70B, and a four-member judge ensemble. Existing splits, prompts, metrics, inference limits, perturbation settings, and the 50-item expert-validation design remain unchanged.

E4.justification: Appendix G.4 extends ensemble-composition checks with two configurations incorporating GPT-OSS-120B, one also including Phi-4. Appendix I expands error categorization and discusses the already-present PILA example more explicitly. Existing perturbation, subgroup, and cross-linguistic analyses are retained.

E5.justification: Both versions use bootstrapped standard errors, the same expert sample, the same Alt-test tolerance levels and multiple-testing correction, and the same cross-linguistic statistical tests. Additional result rows introduce no new uncertainty-reporting practice or repeated-run information.

E6.justification: v6 adds ten open-question result rows, five MCQ rows, corresponding individual-judge scores, and two ensemble Alt-test results. Claude-4.5-Sonnet scores 62.76 on open questions and 58.01% on MCQs, placing second on MCQs. New ensembles achieve winning rate 1.00 with advantage probabilities 0.760 and 0.740. All 26 retained models' headline scores and standard errors match v4.

T1.justification: No new formal definitions, assumptions, derivations, or proofs are introduced. The Alt-test's mathematical setup is retained; expanded discussion of legal reasoning is conceptual explanation.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction's four contributions, and conclusion retain the same claims about benchmark difficulty, process- and outcome-based evaluation, and scalable expert-validated judging. Additional results support these existing claims.

C2.justification: v6 explicitly qualifies English–German performance comparisons because the questions are not parallel translations, explains the absence of human exam-solving baselines, and elaborates the judge's doctrinal and bias-mitigation rationale. Appendix G.4 adds a cost-based explanation for retaining the original ensemble, while Appendix I expands interpretations of legal errors.

D1.justification: v6 newly documents question retention, perturbation-subset selection, and the independent origins of English and German questions. New Table 10 supplies perturbation counts by course. These are documentation additions; Appendix F's hyperparameters, hardware, costs, and the stated code/data access remain unchanged.

R1.justification: v6 adds references for the newly evaluated model families and releases. Section 3.1 explicitly disclaims novelty for the ensemble evaluation paradigm and positions it as a practical validated application. Section 6 and the comparison with prior legal datasets remain substantively unchanged.

P1.justification: Selected paragraphs in Sections 2–4 and Appendices E.2, G.4, and I are expanded or refined. Course and metadata terminology receive corrections, and an author gains equal-contribution credit. The overall section order and most prose remain intact.

P2.justification: v4's combined Table 1 is split into v6's open-question Table 1 and appendix MCQ Table 11. v6 adds the course-count Table 10 and expands judge-result tables. Figures 4–5 are restyled and resized with unchanged plotted values and error bars; other displays are largely retained or relocated.

improvement.justification: The additional model and ensemble comparisons broaden the benchmark's empirical usefulness, while clearer selection documentation and explicit qualification of English–German comparisons improve interpretability. Gains remain limited: expert validation still uses the same 50 items, and new documentation contains minor inconsistencies, including ten courses in Section 2.1.2 versus eleven listed in Table 10.
